sections.title: Why washing needs more than water
paragraphs: Oil on a plate presents a problem for water. A stream can move loose crumbs and carry away substances that dissolve readily, but it may run around a film of oil without removing much of it. The two liquids tend to remain separate. Scrubbing can shift some of the oil physically, although the displaced material may spread to another part of the plate. An effective wash needs a way to loosen the film and carry it away. The distinction between loosening and removal matters. A plate may look cleaner where the brush has just passed while some of the material has merely been moved to another surface.

Soap molecules have regions that interact differently with water and with oil. One end can remain in contact with water, while the other is more readily associated with oily material. When a film is broken into small droplets, molecules can arrange themselves around the droplets in a way that helps keep them dispersed. Water can then carry the small droplets away instead of letting them gather into a continuous film again. The important change is therefore not that the oil has ceased to exist. It is that the oil has been divided and held in a form that can leave the surface with the wash water.

The action of a brush or cloth can help this process by exposing new parts of the film. A thick layer gives water and soap access mainly at its boundary. Breaking the layer up increases the area where the liquids meet. The cleaning material can then reach more of the oil. This is one reason soaking and gentle movement can work together. Soaking gives water and soap time to reach an area, while movement helps detach material and replace liquid that has already taken up dirt. A delicate surface may tolerate a longer soak better than hard scrubbing, although the choice also depends on whether the material can safely remain wet.

Temperature can influence the process without acting as a substitute for it. Some fats become easier to move when they warm because they become softer or less thick. Water at a suitable temperature can therefore help loosen a film. An object that is sensitive to heat may need another approach, and a hot rinse by itself may leave a layer after the water has drained away. The cleaning step still needs to separate the oily material from the surface. The maker of a washing method has to weigh the convenience of warming the water against the demands of the object and the conditions under which it is being cleaned.

Water can contain dissolved substances that affect the performance of soap. Calcium and magnesium in hard water can react with ordinary soap to form material that is less readily carried away. This can leave a deposit and reduce the amount of soap available to interact with the dirt. If a cleaning method performs differently in two buildings, the type of water is one possible explanation. Comparing the same object and the same amount of soap under similar conditions can help isolate the effect. It is better to check the water than to assume that a product will behave identically wherever it is used.

Rinsing removes the liquid that contains loosened material. A cloth used on one area can carry that liquid to another, especially if it has not been rinsed itself. In some tasks, replacing dirty wash water matters more than adding another measure of soap to the original water. A final rinse also helps remove cleaning material that would otherwise remain when the surface dries. The point is to check the whole path taken by the dirt, from the original film through the wash liquid to the place where that liquid is removed. A method that stops after the film is loosened has completed only part of the task.

To compare two washing methods, an investigator can prepare similar surfaces, apply comparable amounts of oil and keep track of the time spent on each step. The observer should decide what counts as a successful result. A surface that looks clear under one light might still feel oily, while a trace left by the soap can look like residual dirt. Using more than one observation can help separate these cases. The results should describe the conditions of the comparison, including the surface and the water. That account is more useful than a general claim that one method always cleans better, because it indicates where the result is likely to apply.

sections.title: A pond beneath its winter cover
paragraphs: When a pond first develops ice, the surface and the water below it are in different conditions. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it remains at the surface rather than sinking as each new piece forms. The layer can reduce the exchange of heat and air between the water and the surroundings. It does not establish that the whole pond is frozen. The depth of liquid water depends on conditions such as the duration of cold weather and the depth of the pond. Looking at the surface alone can therefore provide a poor guide to the space that remains available to organisms beneath it.

Fresh water has an unusual relation between temperature and density near freezing. Water at about four degrees Celsius is denser than water close to zero. In a quiet pond that is cooling, water around that denser state can lie below colder water nearer the surface. This arrangement is one reason why a pond can freeze from the top while deeper water remains liquid. Wind, movement of water and the shape of the pond can complicate the pattern before a stable cover forms. An account based on temperature needs to state how far below the surface each measurement was taken and whether the water was being disturbed.

Ice also changes the way light enters the pond. Clear ice can transmit some light, while a snow layer can reflect or absorb enough to make the water underneath noticeably darker. The thickness and condition of the cover matter. A patch swept clear by wind can admit more light than a nearby patch buried in snow. Organisms capable of photosynthesis may continue producing oxygen where light remains sufficient. Their activity can be limited where the cover is darker. Observations of one point should therefore be related to the local condition of the surface rather than automatically treated as representative of the whole pond.

Oxygen can continue to be used during the period of ice cover. Animals need it for respiration, and organisms breaking down dead material also consume it. If little enters from the air and photosynthesis is weak, the amount available in the water may decline. This does not happen at the same rate in every pond. The amount of material being decomposed, the duration of the cover and the supply of light are all relevant. A study that records only the date on which the ice formed would miss differences that help explain why organisms survive one winter but struggle during another.

Parts of the pond can remain connected to moving water. A small inflow or outlet can keep conditions near one edge different from those in a sheltered centre. The moving water may have a different temperature or carry a different concentration of dissolved oxygen. Measuring beside the inlet could therefore give a result that does not describe the more isolated part of the pond. A useful survey can compare fixed points across the site and record why those points were chosen. If a value changes, the observer can then ask whether the change is widespread or mainly associated with the movement of water at one location.

The bottom of the pond influences conditions too. Leaves and other organic material can accumulate there after autumn. Where the material is being decomposed, the oxygen near the bottom may behave differently from that higher in the water. A surface reading will not describe this difference. Taking measurements at several depths helps reveal whether low oxygen affects only part of the water or extends through much of it. The results can be compared with observations of animals moving to different levels. A change in their location may reflect the conditions they encounter rather than a change in the number of animals present.

When the ice breaks up, the processes affecting the pond change again. Wind can move the surface water and help mix it with water lower down. Air and light can reach places that were separated from them by ice and snow. The date of thaw is useful, but it should be read alongside information about the winter cover and conditions within the pond. A short period of open water may be enough to change some observations before others respond. Recording the sequence helps distinguish the effects of the winter cover from the changes that follow its disappearance. It also gives a clearer basis for comparing one winter with the next.

sections.title: Comparing a translation with its source
paragraphs: Readers often ask whether a translation is faithful. The question is easier to answer if the aspect of the text under discussion is specified. A sentence can report an event, establish a relationship between speakers and create a particular rhythm at the same time. Preserving its sequence of words as closely as possible may help with some of these features while making others difficult to reproduce. A translation intended for a reader studying the language may therefore make different choices from one intended to be read aloud. The writer treats fidelity as a question about which effects can be preserved under particular conditions.

An idiom shows the problem clearly. A phrase made of ordinary words may have a conventional meaning that is not apparent from those words in isolation. Translating each word can produce a sentence that is grammatically clear while giving the wrong impression of what the speaker meant. Replacing the phrase with a conventional expression in the receiving language may preserve the intention. It can also replace an image that matters elsewhere in the text. If the original expression refers to a tool that returns in the story, removing the tool from the translated phrase can make a later connection harder for the reader to recognise.

A dialogue can create a second difficulty. A speaker may choose a form of address that marks respect, distance or familiarity. The receiving language may not make the same distinction with a single word. The translator can sometimes suggest it through the form of a request or the amount of explanation the speaker gives. This shifts the evidence for the relationship from one feature of the sentence to another. A comparison that checks only whether the same kind of word was used would miss that shift. It is more helpful to ask whether the reader can infer a similar relationship from the resources available in the new version.

Some translations preserve an ambiguity deliberately. A line might be understood in two ways, and the uncertainty might be important to the way a later event is read. Choosing one meaning too early can remove an effect even if the chosen meaning is defensible. On the other hand, a translation can introduce a new ambiguity simply because a word has several uses in the receiving language. In that case, the new uncertainty may draw attention to a choice the original never offered. An evaluation should distinguish maintaining an existing openness from accidentally creating a different one. Both can lead to multiple readings, but they do different work.

Notes can help a translation preserve something that is hard to carry in the main text. A note can explain an image, record an alternative meaning or show why a detail has been left unfamiliar. This allows the reader to inspect the choice. However, a note interrupts the pace if it has to be consulted while a scene is unfolding. The writer favours using notes where the additional information matters to the purpose of the edition. A reader comparing historical references may value more explanation than a listener hearing a continuous performance. The choice of placing information in the text or beside it is itself part of translation.

A comparison between versions should also consider what the reader already knows. A place name can bring a set of associations to one audience and very few to another. Explaining those associations can make a scene easier to follow, but it can also make the translated sentence more explicit than the source. Leaving the name unexplained preserves its brevity and may preserve its unfamiliarity for some readers. Neither result can be judged solely by counting words. The significance of the change depends on the role of the name in the passage and on the knowledge that the edition reasonably expects its readers to bring to it.

Rather than asking one translated sentence to satisfy every possible purpose, a reviewer can state the feature under examination and compare how the two versions convey it. For a joke, the feature might be the timing of a surprise. For a description, it might be the order in which details become visible. Identifying the feature makes the comparison easier to check, because other readers can point to the same places and dispute the interpretation if necessary. A strong evaluation can acknowledge a useful choice and a resulting loss in the same sentence. This recognises that the effects of a translation may differ without reducing the comparison to a single verdict.
